ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: A child who tends cattle: a herdboy, cowherd boy, or oxherd boy.
EvidenceBody: The term occurs 334 times in 139 allowlisted texts, and Chan records concentrate its distinctive use in oxherding songs, pictures, public questions, and verse. In Puming's ten oxherding verses, the boy holds the grass rope without slack and works all day; later, when there is no ox anywhere, the boy is idle, claps, sings under the moon, and still returns to “one further barrier.” Fenyang Shanzhao's Herdboy Song says that the boy does not copy texts or read a single graph, yet unfolds countless scrolls and handles question and answer. Asked “what is the herdboy's song?” Xuefeng Yicun dances and leaves the teaching hall. Jiashan Lingquan Ziying answers “who is the person within Jiashan's scene?” with “the herdboy sings in the open fields; the woodcutter laughs deep in the clouds.” Dizang Shouen, Danxia Zichun, Hongzhi Zhengjue, and Furong Daokai further place the boy in teaching-seat and portrait verse. Zen bends the ordinary cattle-tending child into a recurring actor in staged ox-and-herder sequences, direct interview answers, and teaching-seat songs; different stages of the same herdboy-and-ox deployment are not separate senses.
